core_principles.text: When done correctly, full squats strengthen the muscles, ligaments, and tendons surrounding the knee.
The core muscles are developed to a large degree by keeping the torso erect during the squat.
Stand under the bar with the bar across the center of the shoulders.
Ensure the entire body is under the bar before lifting.
Prior to lifting the bar, inhale to expand the lungs and hold until you have set up.
Stand erect with the chest filled with air.
Take only one or two steps backward to set up.
Grip the bar with a closed, pronated grip.
A closer grip activates the muscles in the back.
Head and eyes should be positioned forward to keep the cervical spine in line with the body and help maintain bodyweight distribution throughout the squat.

common_mistakes.text: Not placing the body in the center of the bar during setup.
Not placing the entire body under the bar during setup.
Not filling the body with air and holding during setup.
Taking more than two steps to set up.
Gripping the plates and not the bar.
Taking hands off the bar during the ascending phase.
Gripping the bar with an open grip.
Tilting the head forward during the squat.
Tilting the head backward during the squat.

specific_findings.text: In a low-bar squat, the bar sits 1 to 2 inches below the deltoids.

consequences.text: Placing the bar in a high-bar position on top of the trapezius muscles near the base of the neck increases force at the knees.
Placing the bar in a low-bar position 1 to 2 inches below the deltoids increases force at the hips.
Tilting the head forward can shift weight to the balls of the feet, placing excess stress on the body, and cause rounding of the back.
Tilting the head backward can shift weight to the heels of the feet, causing an improper curvature of the spine and unwanted stress on the neck and back.

core_principles.text: Inhale deeply to maintain intra-thoracic pressure and prevent bending forward, arching the back, and passing out.
The torso should be held between 35 and 45 degrees from vertical.
The back should be kept flat and straight throughout the movement.
Proper depth is achieved when the mid-thigh is parallel to the floor.
Never flex the spine or round forward during a squat.
Keep knees pointed out, aligned with the feet, and behind the toes throughout the entire lift.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the torso to lean too far forward.
Not squatting with a rigid torso.
Rounding the back during the descent.

specific_findings.text: Point toes out slightly from neutral to 30 degrees.
The torso should be held between 35 and 45 degrees from vertical.
If the torso is held at less than 35 degrees from vertical, you are too upright.
If the torso is held at more than 45 degrees from vertical, you are leaning too far forward.

consequences.text: Failing to inhale deeply can cause the lifter to bend forward, arch the back, or pass out due to a loss of intra-thoracic pressure.
Failing to maintain an erect position during a front squat causes the bar to roll forward.
Weak or unengaged abdominal muscles reduce torso stability and intra-thoracic pressure during the squat.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the knees to come together in a valgus knee position during movement increases the strain on the joint.

consequences.text: Allowing the knees to come together (valgus knee position) increases the strain on the ligaments and muscles surrounding the knee.

core_principles.text: When performing a countermovement (rapid, shallow squat), the hips, knees, and ankles should create a straight line when viewed from the front.
